The thesis

Enterprise marketing does not have an ideas problem. It has an execution problem.

Every large marketing organization I sold into had the same shape of failure. The strategy was sound, the creative was ready, and the campaign still took three weeks because the content lived in one system, the customer data lived in another, the brand and accessibility review lived in a queue, and no single person could see the whole path from idea to live. Marketing teams were not short of tools. They were short of a place where the work actually got done.

01

Execution is where the value leaks

I watched enterprise clients invest heavily in data platforms and engagement tools, then lose the return in the handoffs between them. The gap was never the model or the message. It was the assembly line.

02

Agents have to work inside the stack

No enterprise marketing organization is going to rip out its content management system, its digital asset manager and its workflow tool. Anything that requires a migration before it delivers value dies in procurement. Executing inside the systems of record is the only version that survives a real enterprise.

03

Governance decides the deal

Demos sell, audits ship. In regulated Canadian enterprises the buying decision is made by whether privacy, brand and compliance can live with how an agent behaves and what it leaves behind in the audit trail. That conversation is where most AI pitches quietly fall apart.

Canada go-to-market

How I would build the Canadian business

An honest first draft, written from outside the company and without customer data in front of me. I would expect to revise most of it after the first thirty customer conversations, which is the point.

Days 0 – 30 · Learn and load
  • Work the existing global accounts with a Canadian footprint first. Amazon Web Services, Prudential, T-Mobile, Vanguard and U.S. Bank all have Canadian or cross-border marketing organizations, and an internal reference is the cheapest pipeline in a new market.
  • Sit in on live implementations to learn where value actually lands versus where the deck says it does.
  • Map the Canadian buying committee: chief marketing officer, marketing operations, digital and content operations, and the privacy and brand governance functions that hold the veto.
  • Build the Canadian reference list I already have. Twelve years of enterprise marketing relationships in this market is the asset I bring on day one.
Days 30 – 90 · Find the wedge
  • Target the three verticals where Canadian content volume, brand risk and regulation collide: national retail and consumer goods, financial services, and telecommunications.
  • Lead with the two problems unique to this market: bilingual content operations, where every asset ships twice, and accessibility compliance, where standards obligations make manual review unsustainable at volume.
  • Run a small number of tightly scoped, instrumented first deployments rather than a wide, thin pilot program. First customers are the playbook.
  • Bring the governance conversation forward, not backward. Put audit trail, human approval gates and data residency on the table in the first meeting instead of the security review.
Days 90 – 180 · Build the machine
  • Turn the first wins into Canadian proof: named references, measured cycle-time reduction, and a repeatable business case a chief marketing officer can take to a chief financial officer.
  • Codify the pattern into a qualification model and a deal structure the next hire can run without me in the room.
  • Define the shape of the Canadian team and hire against evidence of what the motion actually needs, not against an assumed org chart.
  • Feed the market signal back to product and leadership. Canadian requirements around bilingual output, data residency and accessibility are product input, not objections to handle.

Market building

In healthcare and life sciences I built the vertical go-to-market myself with very little enablement, then co-authored the account-based marketing model the global sales organization adopted. Separately, I built Salesforce's national employee network for Black professionals in Canada from zero to more than 500 members.

Leadership

As a Director I led a ten-person team across six offices delivering better than 30% of my organization's vertical revenue. Before Salesforce, three and a half years of first-line people management at Enterprise Rent-A-Car with full profit-and-loss ownership across two branches.

AI credibility

Pre-release, not press-release

I served as a field evaluator for Salesforce's agentic AI platform before general availability, co-determining enterprise readiness. I have had the difficult version of the AI conversation with enterprise buyers, including the ones who said no and told me exactly why.

How I lead

A revenue operating system, not a set of workshops

Buyers have moved. IDC research finds about 70% of B2B technology buyers expect to rely more on AI tools than on salespeople, so they arrive pre-informed and with a short list. Gated, repetitive qualification loses them. The leader's job is system design: one shared language, one inspection standard and one prospecting craft, wired into a single cadence measured on pipeline and win rate. I map it to the same four layers I use to read any enterprise stack.

Context

Clean pipeline and win/loss data

A forecast is only as good as the data under it. Clean stage history, win and loss reasons and competitor tags come first, so every call is grounded in evidence rather than optimism.

Work

MEDPICC deal inspection

Every deal is inspected against MEDPICC. A missing economic buyer or champion is flagged and coached to the gap. Sandler sets the qualification discipline, mutual agreements and no happy ears, run inside a motion the buyer controls.

Agency

AI-assisted research and prep, governed

Agents should handle account research, meeting prep and first drafts so sellers spend their time with customers, with clear rules on what data an agent can touch and who signs off on what it produces.

Engagement

Intelligence in the seller's flow

Deal signals and competitive plays belong where reps already work, in the team's workspace, whether that is Slack or Teams, not in another dashboard nobody opens.

Prospecting

A process, not a mood

Every email I write uses the BASHO framework from Filling the Funnel, and every prospecting call follows the same structure. In a new market with little inbound demand, that consistency is what builds the first pipeline.

Competition

Differentiation is proven in the deal

I have competed against Adobe, Oracle, Microsoft, HubSpot, Marketo and Braze in enterprise deals. When every vendor claims AI, deals default to price or familiarity unless the seller carries a sharp, evidence-based competitive story. That story gets built, rehearsed and inspected like any other part of the pipeline.
